title: An earlier video said the heat pump tax credit ran through 2033. The IRS says it ended in 2025.

sentences.text: In an earlier video, The Thought Provocateur told viewers, "technically these heat pump tax credits based on the bill that was signed are available through 2033".

assertions.text: In an earlier video, The Thought Provocateur said that technically these heat pump tax credits, based on the bill that was signed, are available through 2033.

quote.text: technically these heat pump tax credits based on the bill that was signed are available through 2033
quote.speaker: The Thought Provocateur

qualifications: s01 dates the quotation and keeps its hedge: "In an earlier video" and the speaker's own "technically", so the Short reports what the channel said about the law as it then stood, never what the law says now.

sentences.note: Revision 3 answers the blocking finding on s01. The quotation is now dated ("In an earlier video", as the parent's s23 does) and the speaker's own hedge "technically" is restored, so a viewer who sees only this Short hears a statement made about the bill as signed, not a claim about today's law; s03 then says the credit was cut short, which is what the IRS passage establishes. The title is reworded to the past tense for the same reason ("ran through 2033"), so it promises no more than the Short delivers. The eyebrow is CLAIM UNDER EXAMINATION, so the Short still opens on the belief in the source's own words and nothing else, with the channel named so the quotation carries a speaker.

sentences.text: The credit was real while it lasted: 30 percent of the cost of a qualifying heat pump, capped at $2,000 a year from 2023.

assertions.text: Beginning January 1, 2023, the home improvement credit equals 30% of qualified expenses, with a maximum of $2,000 per year for qualified heat pumps.
qualifications: s02 keeps the cap beside the rate and now gives the rate its measure: 30 percent of the cost of a qualifying heat pump but no more than $2,000 in any one year, and only from 2023, which is the first carry the parent made elsewhere.

sentences.note: Carries the first qualification the parent video made in s24: the credit existed and was worth something definite, so the Short never implies the viewer was promised nothing. Revision 3 restores the denominator the warning asked for, "30 percent of the cost of", the wording of both the package's carry and the parent's s24; nothing else in the sentence changed.

sentences.text: But it was cut short: the IRS says it is not allowed for any property placed in service after December 31, 2025; a qualifying heat pump in service before that deadline can still claim it.

assertions.text: The IRS says the 25C energy efficient home improvement credit, whose termination was accelerated, will not be allowed for any property placed in service after December 31, 2025.
qualifications: s03 now says in the narration what the assertion already carried: the credit was cut short, its termination accelerated, and what ended is the federal credit, only for property placed in service after December 31, 2025, so a heat pump in service by that date is not affected.

assertions.text: The IRS says the credit is allowed for qualifying property placed in service on or after January 1, 2023 and before December 31, 2025.
qualifications: s03 is itself the carry, and it now keeps the passage's word "qualifying": the same sentence that says the credit is gone says who can still claim it, the owner of a qualifying heat pump in service before the deadline.

sentences.note: Two assertions because the sentence makes two independent claims: that the credit is not allowed after the date, and that a qualifying heat pump in service before it can still claim the credit. The second half is the parent's qualification, kept in the same breath as the first so a conditional result does not become an absolute one. Revision 3 answers the blocking finding by restoring the parent's "But it was cut short", the clause the cited passage already entails ("OBBB accelerated the termination") and the assertion already carried, so the Short does not leave a viewer believing the credit was never available past 2025 or that the quoted channel invented 2033. It also answers the warning on s03.b: the passage reads "allowed for qualifying property" and the same page conditions 2025 claims on a qualified manufacturer and a QMID, so the narration says "a qualifying heat pump" and "can still claim it" rather than stating entitlement outright. The narration pins no boundary day: the IRS's own two pages differ on whether December 31 itself qualifies, and the Short does not need to settle it. No year after 2025 is spoken as current, because no cited passage names one.

sentences.text: And what ended is federal: the IRS lists it by code section, 25C beside 25D; state and utility rebates are separate programmes.

assertions.text: The IRS fact sheet lists the accelerated terminations by code section: 25C, the energy efficient home improvement credit, and 25D, the residential clean energy credit; the entries it gives are federal credits, and it names no state or utility rebate programme.
qualifications: s04 carries the third qualification beside what it limits: the thing that ended is the federal credit the IRS lists by code section, and state and utility rebates are separate programmes, on which this Short says nothing either way.

sentences.note: Revision 3 answers the warning by dropping the argument from absence. "With no state or utility rebate on the list" invited the inference that rebates are the surviving route, which the package's own DOE Program Notice 26-2 shows is wrong for a viewer replacing a gas furnace, and which this Short has no room to answer. The sentence now makes the same carry positively: what the IRS ended is the federal credit it lists by code section, and state and utility rebates are separate programmes. It does not say any rebate is still open; the package holds no verdict on one, and its gaps say so.

sentences.text: What a heat pump really costs is the question the full inquiry takes on.
